item.title: Entity Framework Core Filtered Include: Strategies and Examples
item.description:
“Entity Framework Core Filtered Include: Strategies and Examples”

Entity Framework Core 5 introduced the capability to filter included navigation properties, allowing for more precise data retrieval. This feature enables the application of Where clauses directly within Include and ThenInclude expressions, significantly improving query efficiency by fetching only necessary related entities.

Supported Operations

The filtered Include supports several LINQ operations:

  • Where: To filter entities based on specific conditions.
  • OrderBy / OrderByDescending: To sort included collections.
  • ThenBy / ThenByDescending: For secondary sorting criteria.
  • Skip: To skip a specified number of elements in the included collection.
  • Take: To retrieve a specified number of elements from the included collection.

Usage Examples and Scenarios

When using filtered Include, it’s crucial to adhere to certain guidelines, especially concerning multiple filters on the same navigation property.

item.title: Entity Framework Querying Composite Keys: Effective Strategies Compared
item.description:
“Entity Framework Querying Composite Keys: Effective Strategies Compared”

Consider a scenario where you need to select entities based on marked pairs of Id1 and Id2:

| Id1 | Id2 | Match | |

Solutions

–|

Id1  Id2
---  ---
1    2 *
1    3
1    6
2    2 *
2    3 *
... (many more)
from entity in db.Table // db is a DbContext
join pair in Tuples on new { entity.Id1, entity.Id2 }
                equals new { Id1 = pair.Item1, Id2 = pair.Item2 }
select entity
from entity in db.Table.AsEnumerable() // fetch db.Table into memory first
join pair Tuples on new { entity.Id1, entity.Id2 }
             equals new { Id1 = pair.Item1, Id2 = pair.Item2 }
select entity
from entity in db.Table
where ids1.Contains(entity.Id1) && ids2.Contains(entity.Id2)
select entity
var computed = ids1.Zip(ids2, (i1,i2) => i1 * i2); // [2,6]
from entity in db.Table
where computed.Contains(entity.Id1 * entity.Id2)
select entity
from entity in db.Table
where computed.Contains("Id1=" + entity.Id1 + "," + "Id2=" + entity.Id2)
select entity
var rawSelection = from entity in db.Table
                   where ids1.Contains(entity.Id1) && ids2.Contains(entity.Id2)
                   select entity;

var refined = from entity in rawSelection.AsEnumerable()
              join pair in Tuples on new { entity.Id1, entity.Id2 }
                              equals new { Id1 = pair.Item1, Id2 = pair.Item2 }
              select entity;

–|

item.title: LINQ Projection to Entity Type: Why the Restriction and Workarounds
item.description:
“LINQ Projection to Entity Type: Why the Restriction and Workarounds”

A common challenge when working with LINQ and Object-Relational Mappers (ORMs) like Entity Framework is the inability to directly project query results into an entity type when using LINQ to Entities. This restriction, while seemingly arbitrary to some, is rooted in how the ORM translates your LINQ queries into SQL and manages the entity’s state.

When you attempt to select new EntityType { ... } within a LINQ to Entities query, the ORM typically encounters an issue because it cannot directly generate SQL that maps to a specific, partially constructed entity instance in the same way it can for anonymous types or Data Transfer Objects (DTOs). The ORM needs to know precisely which properties to fetch and how to materialize them into an object that can potentially be tracked by the ORM’s change tracker.

item.title: LINQ Left Outer Joins Explained: Syntax and Examples
item.description:
“LINQ Left Outer Joins Explained: Syntax and Examples”

When querying data from multiple sources in C# using LINQ, effectively combining related information while ensuring all records from a primary source are retained is crucial. This is precisely what a left outer join accomplishes. It includes all records from the “left” table and the matching records from the “right” table. If no match is found in the right table, null values (or default values) are used for the right table’s columns.
